name: Amis
confidence_why: 9 sources read support the record, but its own quotation is not confirmed first-hand
sweep_summary: One Glottolog title matched this search of works with stress in the title: Bril & Skopeteas, 'The syntax and prosody of focus in Northern Amis (Formosan)' (published Faits de Langues 52(1): 61-87, 2021, not 2020 as Glottolog has it). It is relevant to word stress and was obtained open: HAL (halshs-03485243) blocks our network with an Anubis bot-check and Brill with a human-verification page, so the author manuscript was pulled from the the Internet Archive snapshot of the HAL file and Sec. 2.1 p. 62 states that primary stress is on the last syllable of the prosodic word, suffixes always attract stress, enclitics are normally unstressed unless focused; secs. 3.3 and 4.4 add that emphatic lengthening/reduplication optionally shifts stress to the penult as a focus device. This refines (and is compatible with) the catalog's 'fixed-dominant' final-stress coding, whose current deciding source is only Wikipedia; it is a peer-reviewed first-hand statement and should replace that source (alongside the Maddieson & Wright 1995 and Wu 2016 originals downloaded on 9/16). A Crossref by-product, Khuat 2026 (Speech Prosody, open on the ISCA archive, also saved), independently confirms word-final stress in Sakizaya and Falangaw Amis and lists further Amis stress literature not in our bibliography (Khuat 2025 JTLL lexical-stress article, Macaulay 2021 CUNY dissertation, Liu 2002 and Ho 2008 NTU theses, Edmondson & Huang 2004); and in the language directory record every file and URL.

new_statements.quote: Primary stress is on the last syllable of Amis words (Edmonson et al. 2005, Bril 2016). Prosodic words contain roots, affixes (including infixes) and functional elements. A fully inflected word makes up a single prosodic unit with final stress assigned from its right edge (generally excluding enclitics, as shown in (1b) where the perfective marker =tu is unstressed). Suffixes always attract stress; compare stress assignment on the root meláw [mǝláw] "see, look", and on the following affixed words melaw-án [mǝ.la.wán] "seen", and ma-melaw-án [ma.mǝ.la.wán] "seen"

new_statements.reading: Final (ultimate) stress on the prosodic word = root + affixes, with suffixes attracting stress and enclitics excluded unless focused; a predictable, dominant final pattern. The only departures are pragmatic: under emphatic lengthening or reduplication the stress often (optionally) moves to the lengthened penult, which the authors treat as focus marking, not lexical stress. This matches the catalog's 'fixed-dominant' (non-strict) final-stress coding and supplies the domain detail (suffixes in, enclitics out) that the catalog record lacks.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Amis falls on the final syllable of the word. Stress is marked with a F0 maximum on the vowel of the final syllable. Some lexical items seem to surface with non-final stress in Amis. One example that recurred in the data provided by Samay is cówa, used as a negator. This word is always produced with stress on the penult rather than the ultima [p. 456] ... Suffixes in Amis are included within the domain of stress. [p. 457] ... I conclude that enclitics are not part of the domain of stress in Amis, and that seeming counterexamples like that in Figure 8.12 may be cases of pitch accent suppression due to position in the utterance and syntactic structure. [p. 461] ... Amis is stress-final. Words are realized with a L+H* pitch accent [p. 475]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the last syllable of the word; the domain is root plus suffixes (the undergoer-voice -en, imperative -en, factual -ay all take the stress), while enclitic pronouns (=iso, =ako) lie outside the domain and may carry their own reduced pitch accent. Stress is realized as an F0 peak (L+H* pitch accent) on the final vowel. Footnote 11: no syllable/mora distinction is needed since each Amis syllable has exactly one moraic segment (no weight sensitivity).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not posited for Amis; the only related remark is that enclitics can host their own (lower-magnitude) pitch accent beside the word's pitch accent (pp. 460-461), which the author treats as pitch accent suppression/reduction rather than secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) The negator cówa is always produced with penultimate stress, 'could be due to simply being a lexical item specified for penultimate stress' (pp. 456-457). (2) The incredulity intonation contour (sec. 8.8.4, pp. 470-475) shifts the F0 peak one syllable leftward onto the penult (e.g. so'elin, waco), an intonational, not lexical, effect; the exclamative particle saw is stressless. (3) Amis is described as having 'possibly no monosyllabic roots' and no evidence for a minimal-word constraint (p. 457, fn. 13).
new_statements.identity_note: Macaulay 2021 ch. 8 describes Southern Amis from one speaker (Samay, language teacher from 'Etolan/Dulan Village, Donghe Township, Taitung County; one-hour recording, p. 441). Wu 2016 describes Central (Siuguluan) Amis. The already-recorded Bril & Skopeteas 2021 describes Northern Amis (Hualien). All three dialect groups agree on final stress, so the glottocode-level coding is unaffected, but the dialect should be stated per source.

new_statements.quote: 在阿美語中，重音落在詞的最後一個音節，故不特別標示。當詞根或詞幹加上詞綴時，重音亦跟著移動，使重音仍落在所成新詞的最後一個音節上，例如加了 -an、-en 等後綴的詞重音會落在後綴。但有的時候，配合是非問句的語調改變或是強調語氣（如元音拉長），重音會移至倒數第二音節，此現象將在下一節討論。一般而言，阿美語的敘述句語調為下降調（即 - - - - ↘ 之調型），但表示是非問句的時候，語調會改變，在最後一個詞的倒數第二音節語調升高並在最後一個音節下降至平調（即 - - - - ↗ - 之調型），此時重音節也會移倒數第二音節。
new_statements.translation: In Amis, stress falls on the last syllable of the word, so it is not specially marked. When a root or stem takes affixes, the stress moves along with them so that it still falls on the last syllable of the newly formed word; for example, in words with the suffixes -an, -en etc. the stress falls on the suffix. But sometimes, in line with the intonation change of a yes/no question or with an emphatic tone (such as vowel lengthening), the stress moves to the penultimate syllable; this phenomenon is discussed in the next section. Generally, the intonation of an Amis declarative sentence is falling (pattern - - - - ↘), but in a yes/no question the intonation changes: on the penultimate syllable of the last word the pitch rises and on the last syllable it falls to a level tone (pattern - - - - ↗ -), and at that time the stressed syllable also moves to the penult.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is always on the final syllable of the (affixed) word, so it is left unmarked in the orthography; suffixes such as -an and -en attract it. The only shifts to the penult are prosodic: yes/no-question intonation or emphatic vowel lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions. Penultimate stress arises only under yes/no-question intonation (rise on the penult of the last word, fall to level on the ultima) or emphasis with vowel lengthening.

sources.quote: 'Amis has stress accent. There are two patterns of stress assignment: the declarative pattern and interrogative pattern. In the declarative pattern, the stress falls on the ultimate syllable of the word, as illustrated in (6) [mi-loklok-ay [mi.lok.lo.'kaj] cf. [mi.lok.'lok]]. This is the unmarked stress assignment in Amis. In the interrogative pattern, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a word ... sources.quote: Stress in the Amis dialects has been described in two patterns. It is typically realized in word-final position with phonetic prominence [3, p.112] [4, 8–9] [5, p.17] [6, p.377] [7, p.264] [8, p.17] [9, p.15], and affixation triggers predicable stress reassignment [5, p.17] [7, p.266] [8, p.17] [9, p.16] [10] [11, ch.4] [12, pp.62–63]. ... In Amis, stress in isolated content words is realized as a word-final falling tone (HL) [13] ... Unlike content words (§3.1), function words, even when disyllabic, do not function as stress-bearing units [5, p.17].
sources.locator: Abstract p. 318; sec. 1 Introduction p. 318; sec. 3.1 'Phonological representation of word-level prominence' p. 319; sec. 6 p. 321
sources.note: Sakizaya and Falangaw Amis: word stress in isolation is consistently word-final (ultimate), realized as a word-final HL fall; affixation re-assigns stress to the new final syllable; function words are not stress-bearing. The penultimate high tone in Falangaw Amis wh-questions and the high tone on imperative particles are analysed as tonal reassociation, not stress shift, since ultimate prominence (duration) is preserved. sources.quote: '在阿美語中，重音落在詞的最後一個音節，故不特別標示。當詞根或詞幹加上詞綴時，重音亦跟著移動，使重音仍落在所成新詞的最後一個音節上，例如加了 -an、-en 等後綴的詞重音會落在後綴。但有的時候，配合是非問句的語調改變或是強調語氣（如元音拉長），重音會移至倒數第二音節' [In Amis stress falls on the last syllable of the word and is therefore not marked; when affixes are added to a root/stem the stress moves so that it still falls on the last syllable of the new word, e.g. with suffixes -an, -en stress falls on the suffix. Sometimes, with yes/no-question intonation or emphasis (vowel lengthening), stress moves to the penult.] p.16 adds that in yes/no questions the penult of the last word carries a pitch rise and 'the stressed s
